summary: Arabic prepositions stand before the noun, and the noun after them is always genitive (-i / -in, see fn.case). The core set: فِي (in, at — where?), إِلَى (to — where to?), مِنْ (from — where from?), عِنْدَ (at someone’s place), مَعَ (with — together with), بِـ (with — a tool or an ingredient; by; for a price), بِدُونِ (without), لِـ (for; belonging to) and عَنْ (about; away from). بِـ and لِـ are single letters written together with the next word (بِالْحَلِيبِ, لِأَخِي). Every preposition takes the pronoun endings: مَعِي (with me), لَكَ (for you), مِنْهُ (from him), فِيهَا (in it), إِلَيْكَ (to you). Arabic chooses by the question: فِي for “where?”, إِلَى for “where to?”, عِنْدَ for “at someone’s”.

blocks.caption: One idea, one preposition: فِي, إِلَى and عِنْدَ split “in / at / to”; مَعَ is company, بِـ a tool or an ingredient.

notes.text: Greek σε covers in, at and to (στο σπίτι, πάω στο σχολείο, στον γιατρό); Arabic splits it: فِي, إِلَى, عِنْدَ. Greek με is مَعَ for company but بِـ for a tool or an ingredient (καφές με γάλα = قَهْوَةٌ بِالْحَلِيبِ).

blocks.caption: The endings are those of كِتَابِي, كِتَابُكَ … (lesson 6). After i or ī the -hu, -hum become -hi, -him (فِيهِ, بِهِمْ); the ى of إِلَى becomes يْ (إِلَيْكَ); the n of مِنْ and عَنْ doubles before -ī and -nā (مِنِّي, عَنَّا); لِـ has a before every ending except -ī (لَكَ, but لِي).

blocks.title: Two “with”s.
blocks.text: مَعَ is company: أَنَا مَعَ صَدِيقِي (I am with my friend). بِـ is a tool, an ingredient or a means: أَكْتُبُ بِالْقَلَمِ (I write with a pen), قَهْوَةٌ بِالْحَلِيبِ (coffee with milk).

notes.text: German mit covers both; Arabic says مَعَ صَدِيقِي (mit meinem Freund) but بِالْقَلَمِ (mit dem Stift).
English “with” covers both: with my friend = مَعَ صَدِيقِي, with a pen = بِالْقَلَمِ.
Spanish con covers both: con mi amigo = مَعَ صَدِيقِي, con leche = بِالْحَلِيبِ.
French avec covers both: avec mon ami = مَعَ صَدِيقِي, but café au lait / avec du lait = قَهْوَةٌ بِالْحَلِيبِ.
Russian splits them too: с другом (with a friend) is مَعَ, and a tool takes the bare instrumental (ручкой), where Arabic uses بِـ: بِالْقَلَمِ.
Vietnamese makes the same split: với for company, bằng for a tool or means — với bạn ≈ مَعَ صَدِيقٍ, bằng bút ≈ بِالْقَلَمِ.

blocks.title: Helping vowels before al-.
blocks.text: مِنْ + الْ → مِنَ الْ (مِنَ السُّوقِ); عَنْ + الْ → عَنِ الْ (عَنِ الْمَدِينَةِ). لِـ + الْ drops the alif: لِلْبَيْتِ (li-l-bayti). فِي, إِلَى, مَعَ, بِدُونِ do not change in writing.

blocks.title: “There is” = a place first.
blocks.text: فِي الْقَرْيَةِ مَدْرَسَةٌ — there is a school in the village. The indefinite noun (مَدْرَسَةٌ) comes after the place and is nominative; no verb is needed. Question: هَلْ فِي الْقَرْيَةِ مَدْرَسَةٌ؟

items.def: a preposition (lit. “a particle of dragging”): it “drags” the noun into the genitive (الْجَرّ)
the noun after a preposition, in the genitive

askYourself: Is it a place where something is (in, at)? → فِي. At a person’s place? → عِنْدَ.
Is there movement towards it? → إِلَى. Away from it, or the origin? → مِنْ.
With a person (company)? → مَعَ. With a tool, an ingredient, a means, or for a price? → بِـ.
For someone, or whose is it? → لِـ (written together). Without? → بِدُونِ. About a topic? → عَنْ.
Does the next word start with al-? → مِنَ الْ…, عَنِ الْ…, لِلْ….
Is the noun after it in the genitive (-i, -in)? Is a pronoun after it? → the ending: مَعِي, لَكَ, فِيهِ, إِلَيْهِ.

traps: “To school” is إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَةِ, “at school” فِي الْمَدْرَسَةِ — فِي never means “to”.
A tool takes بِـ, not مَعَ: *أَكْتُبُ مَعَ الْقَلَمِ → أَكْتُبُ بِالْقَلَمِ.
*مِنْ الْبَيْتِ → مِنَ الْبَيْتِ; *عَنْ الْمَدِينَةِ → عَنِ الْمَدِينَةِ.
بِـ and لِـ never stand alone: بِالْحَلِيبِ, لِأَخِي, لَكَ.
“Mine” is لِي, not *لِأَنَا; “for you” لَكَ, not *لِأَنْتَ.
The noun after a preposition is never nominative: *فِي الْبَيْتُ → فِي الْبَيْتِ.

quiz.why: “At” a place, where something is: فِي.
Movement towards a place: إِلَى — in the question too.
An ingredient takes بِـ (مَعَ الْحَلِيبِ is also heard, but never with a nominative الْحَلِيبُ).
لِـ (for) is written together with the next word.
Before al- مِنْ becomes مِنَ, and the noun is genitive (-i).
After a preposition a pronoun is an ending: مَعِي, مَعَكَ, مَعَهُ …
فِي answers “where?”, إِلَى “where to?”, عِنْدَ “at someone’s place”.

seeAlso.note: Hebrew writes its three commonest prepositions together with the noun — בְּ (in), לְ (to, for), מִ (from) — where Arabic attaches only بِـ and لِـ; Hebrew בְּ is the everyday “in”, Arabic says فِي. Hebrew עִם (with) is Arabic مَعَ with the letters swapped.

German keeps one preposition and changes the case: in der Schule (where?) / in die Schule (where to?). Arabic keeps one case (the genitive) and changes the preposition: فِي الْمَدْرَسَةِ / إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَةِ.
Chinese uses coverbs before the verb: 在 (at, in), 从 (from), 跟 (with), 给 (for); the noun after them never changes. Arabic prepositions are followed by the genitive.
Why the noun ends in -i after every preposition: the genitive.

notes.text: French chez is Arabic عِنْدَ: chez le médecin = عِنْدَ الطَّبِيبِ. But French à covers both “at” and “to” (à l’école), where Arabic splits فِي / إِلَى.
Spanish en / a / de match فِي / إِلَى / مِنْ (en casa, a la escuela, de la ciudad).
Russian keeps в and changes the case: в школе (where?) / в школу (where to?); Arabic changes the preposition: فِي الْمَدْرَسَةِ / إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَةِ.
English at / to / from match فِي / إِلَى / مِنْ; “at the doctor’s” is عِنْدَ الطَّبِيبِ.
Turkish marks place, direction and source with case endings (evde, okula, şehirden); Arabic puts prepositions before the noun: فِي الْبَيْتِ, إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَةِ, مِنَ الْمَدِينَةِ.
Hindi postpositions follow the noun (घर में, शहर से); Arabic prepositions come first: فِي الْبَيْتِ, مِنَ الْمَدِينَةِ.

Persian prepositions also come first — در (in), به (to), از (from), با (with), برای (for), بی (without) — and match فِي, إِلَى, مِنْ, مَعَ, لِـ, بِدُونِ almost one to one; only با covers both company and tool, where Arabic splits مَعَ / بِـ.
Marathi uses endings and postpositions after the noun (घरात, in the house); Arabic puts a preposition before it: فِي الْبَيْتِ.
Japanese particles follow the noun (家に, 学校へ, 町から); Arabic prepositions come before it (فِي الْبَيْتِ, إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَةِ, مِنَ الْمَدِينَةِ).
Korean particles follow the noun (집에, 학교에); Arabic prepositions come before it.
Finnish uses case endings — talossa (in), taloon (into), talosta (out of); Arabic uses prepositions and one case after them: فِي الْبَيْتِ, إِلَى الْبَيْتِ, مِنَ الْبَيْتِ.
Hungarian uses case endings — házban, házba, házból; Arabic uses prepositions and keeps the noun in the genitive.
Swahili also has prepositions before the noun (kwa, na) and a locative ending -ni (nyumbani, at home); Arabic uses prepositions only: فِي الْبَيْتِ.
Luganda puts mu (in) and ku (on, at) before the noun, as Arabic does with فِي and عَلَى.
Inuktitut uses case endings: illumi (in the house), illumut (to the house), illumit (from the house); Arabic uses prepositions: فِي الْبَيْتِ, إِلَى الْبَيْتِ, مِنَ الْبَيْتِ.
